supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Monday, November 23, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Survey Shows Public Awareness Remains Low as U.S. Mpox Cases Persist by November 19, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Survey Shows Public Awareness Remains Low as U.S. Mpox Cases Persist Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Four years following the major global outbreak in 2022, the United States continues to record a persistent, low level of mpox cases, yet American public awareness and knowledge concerning the viral disease have changed little over the past two years according to a new nationally representative survey released by the Annenberg Public Policy Center of the University of Pennsylvania. In the latest survey wave, concluded in October 2026, only 8 percent of adults in the United States reported having seen, read, or heard anything about mpox during the preceding month. This figure represents a slight decline from the 11 percent observed in July 2024 and marks a dramatic reduction from the 80 percent recorded in July 2022, when the initial global outbreak drew intensive national and international media coverage. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, domestic transmission patterns have evolved since the acute surge in 2022, with nationwide case counts falling substantially while a steady baseline of infections has endured. The agency has noted that this continued low-level transmission indicates a probable transition toward endemic viral circulation within the country. Federal surveillance data cited in the report show that 1,369 cases of mpox, historically referred to as monkeypox, had been officially confirmed and reported across the United States in 2026 as of October 24. The public health agency emphasizes that the mpox virus spreads person-to-person primarily through close contact, including intimate or sexual contact, with the rash, scabs, or bodily fluids of an infected individual. Secondary transmission routes highlighted by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention include physical contact with contaminated materials such as shared clothing, bedding, towels, and dishes. Furthermore, exposure can occur through direct interaction with small wild animals indigenous to West and Central Africa, where the pathogen has long been established. The survey findings stem from the Annenberg Science and Public Health survey conducted between September 22 and October 5, 2026, among a sample of 1,842 empaneled American adults. Researchers found that widespread knowledge deficits documented during their 2024 assessment remain largely entrenched, following a steep drop from the heightened public attentiveness of 2022. Overall familiarity with the viral infection is notably limited, with merely 24 percent of respondents indicating that they are somewhat or very familiar with mpox, which is statistically unchanged from the 23 percent reported in July 2024. Conversely, 76 percent of surveyed adults indicated that they are not too familiar or not at all familiar with the illness, while only 7 percent expressed worry about personally contracting mpox over the subsequent three months, compared with 5 percent in 2024 and 21 percent in August 2022. General comprehension regarding preventive medical interventions has similarly stagnated over the two-year monitoring interval. Less than half of respondents, or 44 percent, were aware that an effective vaccine against mpox is currently available, a figure virtually identical to the 45 percent measured in 2024 and substantially lower than the 61 percent recorded in August 2022. Nearly half of the public, representing 48 percent, stated that they were unsure whether any vaccine existed. Additionally, only 18 percent of participants correctly identified mpox as being less contagious than the virus causing Covid-19, essentially matching the 17 percent measured in 2024, while 62 percent admitted uncertainty, contrasting with the 41 percent who correctly understood relative contagiousness during the 2022 outbreak. Public recognition of groups facing disproportionate epidemiological risk also showed no meaningful gain. Approximately one-third of respondents, or 33 percent, correctly recognized that men who have sex with men face a higher risk of acquiring an mpox infection, mirroring the 34 percent documented in 2024 and standing at roughly half of the 63 percent who recognized this vulnerability in August 2022, with 53 percent remaining unsure. Awareness of specific transmission pathways showed comparable stagnation: 49 percent recognized that sharing bedding, towels, or clothing used by an infected patient elevates infection risks, compared with 48 percent in 2024, while 51 percent recognized the infection hazard posed by close face-to-face interaction, compared with 49 percent in the previous survey. The persistence of these public knowledge deficits presents distinct public health challenges as the viral pathogen continues to circulate. Ken Winneg, managing director of survey research at the Annenberg Public Policy Center, noted that the stability of these gaps is concerning because the pathogen itself has not stood still. Winneg underscored that as the epidemiology of mpox continues to shift over time, broader public understanding regarding vulnerable populations, viral transmission pathways, and the preventive protection offered by immunization must keep pace with ongoing disease dynamics. Despite broad stagnation across many survey metrics, the research team identified measurable gains in two specific public health domains. Knowledge that the mpox virus can be transmitted through the placenta of an infected pregnant individual rose to 29 percent among American adults, up from 21 percent in July 2024, although 63 percent of respondents still reported being unsure. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention confirms that the virus can transfer to a developing fetus during pregnancy, potentially generating significant health complications for both the pregnant parent and the infant. Concurrently, public awareness regarding recommended infection control practices improved, with 73 percent recognizing that infected individuals should isolate at home until all skin rashes have resolved, compared with 68 percent in 2024. The federal health agency specifically advises patients to remain in isolation until rashes have fully healed, scabs have completely sloughed off, and an intact layer of fresh skin has developed. Intentions to accept vaccination in the event of confirmed exposure remain robust among the American public. The survey revealed that 69 percent of adults would be somewhat or very likely to receive an mpox vaccine if exposed to the pathogen, matching the 68 percent reported in 2024, while an additional 2 percent reported having already received vaccination. Notably, the share of respondents indicating that they would be very likely to seek vaccination climbed significantly from 38 percent in 2024 to 44 percent in the current survey. Furthermore, 73 percent of respondents affirmed that the clinical benefits of mpox vaccination outweigh potential risks, compared with 70 percent in 2024, a change that did not reach statistical significance. In its clinical guidance, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends a two-dose regimen of the JYNNEOS vaccine to achieve maximum protection among recommended populations, noting that the vaccine provides substantial disease prevention and can be administered post-exposure to avert illness. The survey also assessed public susceptibility to unverified narratives and medical falsehoods surrounding mpox origin and immunization. Belief in the unsubstantiated claim that the mpox virus was bioengineered in a laboratory setting was endorsed by 16 percent of respondents as definitely or probably true, showing no meaningful change from 15 percent in 2024, with 41 percent unsure and 43 percent correctly evaluating the statement as false. FactCheck.org, an initiative of the Annenberg Public Policy Center, has extensively debunked this claim. Meanwhile, 7 percent of respondents mistakenly believed that receiving a Covid-19 vaccine increases susceptibility to mpox, statistically unchanged from 6 percent in 2024. However, 63 percent correctly rejected this false claim, improving from 58 percent in 2024, while 30 percent expressed uncertainty. Wave 31 of the Annenberg Science and Public Health survey was administered from September 22 to October 5, 2026, through SSRS, an independent research organization. The study gathered data from 1,842 adults nationwide using both web-based and telephone interviews drawn from the probability-based SSRS Opinion Panel, with post-stratification weighting applied to align results with United States adult demographic parameters. The survey carries a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 3.2 percentage points. The Annenberg Public Policy Center, established in 1993, has monitored public knowledge, beliefs, and behaviors regarding infectious diseases and health communication since April 2021, with this survey project conducted by Winneg alongside Patrick E. Jamieson, Laura A. Gibson, and Kathleen Hall Jamieson. supplementary_news.title: 柬埔寨时隔两年多再现猴痘确诊病例
supplementary_news.excerpt: 中新网金边11月22日电 (张堰林 杨强)柬埔寨卫生部当地时间22日发布通报称,该国近日发现1例猴痘确诊病例,目前患者正在医院接受治疗。 柬埔寨卫生部在通告中表示,前述病例是柬埔寨在过去两年半无新增猴痘感染病例后,再次报告的首例。2023年12月12日至2024年5月14日期间,柬埔寨累计报告20例猴痘确诊病例。
